outcome: The general conjecture (for arbitrary abstract elementary classes, in ZFC, with no extra hypotheses) remains unresolved; work since 26 January 2024 continues the pre-existing pattern of partial/special-case results (tameness, primes, modules, specific successor-cardinal or successive-cardinal setups) rather than settling the stated conjecture.
summary: Shelah's eventual categoricity conjecture for abstract elementary classes (AECs) — that for every λ there is a μ(λ) such that any AEC with Löwenheim–Skolem number ≤ λ categorical in some cardinal above μ(λ) is categorical in all cardinals above μ(λ) — is not resolved in general, and I found no post-26-January-2024 source claiming otherwise. The strongest prior claim, Christian Espíndola's 'A proof of Shelah's eventual categoricity conjecture and an extension to accessible categories with directed colimits' (arXiv:1906.09169), was first posted in June 2019 and last revised April 2022 — entirely before the frozen revision's date, so it cannot be a change within this window even though it remains on arXiv unretracted; if it were to be treated as the state of the art, that would make this an open_stale case, but it is not: the conjecture is still listed and treated as open in current secondary sources (e.g. the Wikipedia 'Abstract elementary class' article states 'As of 2014, the original conjecture remains open,' and no paper I found treats it as settled), and Espíndola's proof does not appear to have been accepted by the model-theory community as a resolution (it is not cited as closing the conjecture in any of the 2024–2026 papers I read, which continue to treat special cases as open problems). Genuinely new work in the window: Mazari-Armida, Vasey and Yang, 'On Stability and Existence of Models in Abstract Elementary Classes' (arXiv:2406.15263, June 2024), which proves a stability/model-existence equivalence and a categoricity theorem for AECs with weak amalgamation and tameness, explicitly built on and improving prior partial results (Vasey 2018, Mazari-Armida–Yang 2024) — a case/refinement, not a resolution of the general conjecture; an untitled 2025 paper on limit models in AECs (arXiv:2503.11605, March 2025) about isomorphism of long/short limit models, adjacent structural theory but not the categoricity conjecture itself; and Anand Pillay's 'Remarks on relative categoricity' (arXiv:2602.05866, February 2026), which proves a case of the distinct 'Gaifman conjecture' on relative categoricity — a related but different notion, not a case of Shelah's AEC conjecture as stated in this bullet. I found no AI system credited anywhere in this literature; a broad search for AI-assisted work on categoricity in AECs or model theory generally returned unrelated LLM-for-mathematics survey/benchmark papers (e.g. Erdős-problem-solving systems, Lean proof search) with no connection to this specific conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue Espíndola's 2019/2022 ZFC proof should count as the resolution, making this problem's correct status 'open_stale' (settled before the frozen revision, list simply stale) rather than 'open'. I did not adopt this reading because the broader model-theory community's secondary literature (surveys, the Wikipedia article on abstract elementary classes, and papers through 2026 that still frame categoricity-transfer results as partial progress toward an open conjecture) does not treat Espíndola's proof as having closed the question — it is not universally accepted the way Morley's theorem or other landmark resolutions are. If a reader instead treats Espíndola's proof as an accepted resolution, the correct status would be open_stale, dated to 2019 (first posting) or 2022 (final ZFC revision), with resolution_direction confirmed and no AI involvement either way.
what_would_settle_it: An explicit statement from a survey, textbook, or leading model theorist (e.g. Vasey, Grossberg, Boney, or Shelah himself) that Espíndola's proof is accepted as resolving the conjecture in full generality — or, alternatively, a specific post-2024 paper stating that a gap was found in Espíndola's argument and that the conjecture remains genuinely open. I found neither an endorsement nor a rebuttal of Espíndola's proof in the accessible literature.
